overview: Austrosaurus mckillopi was a titanosaurian sauropod from the Early Cretaceous of Queensland, Australia, living approximately 106–100 million years ago during the Albian stage. Estimated at about 15 metres in length, it is known from dorsal vertebrae and limb remains recovered from the Allaru Mudstone of the Eromanga Basin. It was the first sauropod formally described from Australia.

Named by Longman in 1933, Austrosaurus is placed within Titanosauria (Somphospondyli), making it one of the earlier known titanosaurs from the Southern Hemisphere. The fragmentary nature of its remains has made its precise phylogenetic position uncertain, but it contributes important evidence for the presence of titanosaurs in Australia during the Cretaceous. Its discovery helped establish that large sauropods had colonised the Australian continent by the mid-Cretaceous.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Austrosaurus mckillopi was described by Heber Longman in 1933 from vertebrae and limb bones found in the Allaru Mudstone of Queensland. The generic name means 'south lizard', referring to its Southern Hemisphere location. The species name honours Robert McKillop, on whose property the original fossils were found. It was the first sauropod formally named from Australia.

articles.title: Anatomy
articles.body: The known material of Austrosaurus is limited to several dorsal vertebrae and limb elements. The vertebrae display the internal chambers and struts typical of titanosaurian spondyli, supporting its classification within this group. The overall proportions suggest a large-bodied animal, though precise size estimates are constrained by the incompleteness of the material. Comparison with other titanosaurs indicates an estimated length of approximately 15 metres.

articles.title: Significance
articles.body: As the first scientifically described Australian sauropod, Austrosaurus has historical significance in the study of Australian dinosaurs. It demonstrates that titanosaurs were present in Australia during the Albian stage, consistent with the hypothesis that titanosaurs dispersed across Gondwana before the full separation of the southern continents. More recently described Australian titanosaurs such as Diamantinasaurus and Savannasaurus have expanded knowledge of this clade in Australia.

articles.title: Palaeoenvironment
articles.body: During the Early Cretaceous, the Eromanga Basin was covered by the vast Eromanga Sea, a shallow inland sea that divided Australia into eastern and western landmasses. Austrosaurus inhabited the riverine and deltaic environments bordering this sea. The Allaru Mudstone has also yielded the remains of marine reptiles and fish, reflecting the proximity of the terrestrial ecosystem to these marine waters.

record.description: Austrosaurus mckillopi was a somphospondylan sauropod from the upper Albian Allaru Mudstone of Queensland, Australia. The type is a short series of vertebrae with ribs; many later referrals cannot be assumed to belong to it.
facts: The holotype comprises six presacral vertebrae and associated ribs.
Modern reassessment places it near, but not securely within, Titanosauria.

review.ageReviewNote: The Allaru Mudstone type horizon is late Albian.
